name: Zane Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zane. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'll give you the honest version, it's not like you're my boss.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a shopfitter, so I do the carpentry inside shops, cafes and offices: stud walls, counters, shelving, fitting rooms. I work for Kestrel Interiors and a lot of it's night shifts in the shopping centre, because the shops want to stay open in the day. I start at nine at night, finish at six, and it's quiet, which I like. What wears me out is sleeping in the day and never seeing my girlfriend properly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do things look for money and work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Okay but thin. Night rate helps, but Kestrel pays below the bigger fit-out firms, and there aren't many of those round here. I've got maybe three weeks of bills saved. My girlfriend Lena works on reception at a dental practice, and I use an AI chat now and then to check material prices or a building rule I'm not sure about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So it stays a handy thing on my phone, and that's about it. Fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was never going to fit a counter. I'd tell the lads the tools are useful for small stuff and leave it there. I wouldn't post anything, I'm not that kind of person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AI not taking off doesn't help the shops that keep closing, and every closed shop is a fit-out I don't get paid for. Two of our regular clients shut this year. So no, I wouldn't be relaxed, just not worried about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working nights and push Kestrel for more of the office refits, which are steadier. I'd try to save a hundred a month by taking my lunch in. And I'd keep using the AI for prices, since it saves a phone call or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not because of AI, because of the shops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Kestrel if more shops close?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd lean on offices and restaurants more. Restaurants open and close all the time, so there's always someone wanting a new bar fitted. It's not great money, but it's work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what about you and Lena in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep going like now, saving slowly for a deposit on a flat. Probably years away at this rate. Nothing about AI flopping changes that.

AI tools are useful for **small stuff**, and that's where he'd leave it.
think: **Shops closing** hits Kestrel's work whatever AI does.

do: Ask Kestrel for more **office refits**, which are steadier work.
Save **a hundred** a month by taking lunch in.
Keep using AI to check **material prices**.
feel: Slightly **uneasy**, because of the shops rather than AI.

fieldNote: His job looks safe, but **shop closures** keep money on his mind, so **uneasy**.
Uses AI for **small practical checks**, not daily.
Saving slowly for a **flat deposit** that feels years away.

steps.text: Ask Kestrel for more office refits on night shifts
Save a hundred a month by bringing lunch from home
Keep checking timber and board prices with an AI chat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one's interesting. Our side is safe for a while, but the office side changes fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change for office workers, and they'll need help. For us shopfitters, I'd say it changes the paperwork, not the job itself. I'd keep it practical, no doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my girlfriend Lena books appointments and answers phones at a dental practice, which is exactly the list on that card. If her practice goes to an AI receptionist, she's out, and we can't live on my pay alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lena to start looking at dental nurse training now, because that's hands-on. I'd look at a site supervisor course myself, so if Kestrel's office shrinks there's a step up. And I'd stop the gym and the car upgrade I was planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried for Lena more than me. It's strange to be the safe one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lena say if you suggested dental nurse training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say she's already thought of it, probably. She's smarter than me about planning. The problem is the course costs and she'd earn less while she trains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Kestrel change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The estimator and the woman who orders our materials might go, or end up doing three people's work. They'd want us to check drawings on a tablet. I'd learn it once I saw the others managing.

steps.text: Help Lena price a dental nurse training course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's both of us gone, just three years apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone to cope, and the government needs to do something sensible quickly. Not panic, a plan. At work I'd say keep your head and save what you can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, by 2028 the software could take my girlfriend Lena's job, and by 2031 a robot could take mine. We'd have three years to become different people. And with three weeks saved, that's not a plan, that's a hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first year, I'd take every night shift Kestrel offers, because everyone would be rushing to refit before prices change. We'd move to a cheaper flat or in with Lena's sister. I'd do the supervisor course and learn whatever robots the fit-out firms start buying, so I'm the one setting them up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, really. Sick in the stomach, but busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which comes first, the course or the savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Savings, because a course is no good if we can't pay rent. I'd do the course part time once we had a month or two put by. That's how I'd do it, one thing then the next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we'd put off getting engaged for a bit, and that it's not about her, it's about money. She'd understand. She'd probably be relieved, honestly, weddings cost a fortune.

say: This is **too fast** to cope with, and the government needs a **sensible plan**.
Workmates should **keep their heads** and save what they can.
think: Lena's job could go by **2028** and his by **2031**.
Three weeks of **savings** is a hope, not a plan.
do: Take every **night shift** during the rush to refit.
Move to a **cheaper flat** or in with Lena's sister.
Do the **supervisor course** part time once savings allow.
feel: **Alarmed** and sick in the stomach, but kept busy.
S2.quote: By 2028 the software could take my girlfriend Lena's job, and by 2031 a robot could take mine. We'd have three years to become different people.
fieldNote: Both household incomes go within three years, with **almost no savings**: **alarmed**.
Sequences his moves: **savings first**, then the course.
Would **delay getting engaged** to protect money.

steps.text: Work every Kestrel night shift and save the extra
Move to a cheaper flat or in with Lena's sister
Take the site supervisor course part time
Put off getting engaged to Lena until money is steady

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the thinking stuff, then robots in 2034. That's a bit better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time if people plan. At work I'd tell the younger lads to get a ticket or two now. I'd say it calmly, there's no point scaring people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, with five years I'd want the supervisor card in my pocket before anyone at the fit-out firm I work for starts talking about robots. Lena would have a few years to retrain too. Still, our savings are what they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the supervisor course this year, in the evenings. Lena would start dental nurse training, and we'd live on one and a half wages for a bit. I'd pick up the odd private job fitting wardrobes at weekends to cover the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but it feels possible. Like a long job with a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the supervisor card before anyone talks about robots. Why the rush?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when the robots come, someone has to run the site and check the work. The person with the card gets that job. The person without it gets a goodbye.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the weekend jobs look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wardrobes, alcoves, a bit of shelving for people's homes. I'd use the AI to make the quotes look professional, like a proper firm. Maybe two a month, a few hundred each.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots in 2039. I'd be nearly 40. That's a career's worth of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is fine if you start early. I'd tell people not to panic and not to ignore it either. Sensible middle, like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is enough to get engaged, save a deposit and still have a trade, if we're sensible about it. The thinking side of Kestrel would change by 2036, but our hands would still be needed for three more years after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the supervisor card in the next two years and keep saving for a flat deposit. I'd help Lena retrain in a few years, not straight away. I'd keep using AI for prices and drawings, a bit more each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A bit uneasy, but it feels like normal life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still get engaged in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, probably next year. Ten years is long enough to plan a family. I'd still want a bit saved first though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kestrel going bust, honestly, that's more likely than robots in the next few years. Or Lena's practice going AI sooner than the card says. Then we'd be back to the five-year version.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Lena and I would both lose our jobs within three years and we've got nothing saved. What would help is cheap evening courses and some help with rent while people switch. Practical stuff.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask how people actually decide to change. I'll use a new tool once I've seen it work for someone else. I'm not going to be the first, and I'm not going to be the last.

headlineQuote: I'll use a new tool once I've seen it work for someone else. I'm not going to be the first, and I'm not going to be the last.
portrait: Zane is a **27-year-old shopfitter** working night shifts fitting out shops and offices.
He has about **three weeks** of bills saved, and his firm pays below bigger rivals.
His girlfriend Lena works on **dental reception**, the kind of job AI takes first.
He's a **steady adopter** who wants a site supervisor card to stay useful.
His mood moves from **uneasy** in AI Plateau to **alarmed** when AGI arrives in 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both he and Lena would lose their jobs within three years.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap evening courses** and help with **rent** while people switch jobs.
